21318-the-lost-middy-being-the-secret-of:
Aleck, a sixteen-year-old orphan, lives by the sea with an uncle whose whole interest is writing a history book. Aleck sails his little boat along the coast with Tom Bodger, a pensioned man-of-war's man. George Manville Fenn then brings a press gang raid to their shore, backed by a revenue cutter.

Local men are seized for the navy. But the smugglers of the hamlet seize a prize of their own: a midshipman from the sloop, hidden in the smugglers' own cave. Aleck stumbles onto their track and is shut in the same cave, both mouths blocked. Fenn leaves his two prisoners in the dark to work the title's secret out.
23195-wikkey-a-scrap:
Wikkey, signed by Yam, tells the story of a young street sweeper. Wikkey is first seen holding his broom beneath a lamp-post where his crossing ends. There he first set eyes on Lawrence Granby, the man on whom the whole tale turns.

The narrator is blunt about that link: had Wikkey never seen Granby, there would be no story to write. Giving the boy another trade, he adds, would not mend matters much. Readers get a Victorian city tale built on one chance meeting between a poor crossing sweeper and a man from a very different world.
3792-capitola-the-madcap:
Emma Southworth continues her Hidden Hand saga in this sequel, with the madcap orphan Capitola at its center. Chapters carry Cap from an orphan's trial to the Hidden House and the Hidden Hollow, where she frees a captive, falls into captivity herself, and spars with the villain Black Donald. Old Hurricane storms, court martials, and a fatal hatred raise the stakes, while a mysterious maniac's story adds a second mystery.

A later scene shows Herbert watching recruits drill, struck by a familiar form in a private's uniform, a lost lover in disguise. Southworth writes at full melodramatic tilt, with disguises, rescues, and reversals on every page. Readers who like Victorian sensation fiction will find Capitola a heroine who never waits to be saved.
5261-constance-dunlap:
Arthur B. Reeve's Constance Dunlap, in the Craig Kennedy series, follows a woman drawn into crime by her husband's troubles. Chapters run through forgers, embezzlers, gun runners, gamblers, eavesdroppers, clairvoyants, plungers, abductors, shoplifters, blackmailers, dope fiends, and fugitives, as Constance learns the underworld from the inside.

The book opens with Carlton Dunlap coming home late, hunted and desperate, and Constance must decide how far to follow him. Reeve gives his heroine unusual agency for a detective tale of the period, and the novel offers a fast tour of early twentieth-century crime, with Kennedy's science in the background.
9151-ruggles-of-red-gap:
Harry Leon Wilson wrote this comic novel in 1915 about Ruggles, an English valet lost in the American West. The tale opens in Paris, where Ruggles tends the Honourable George with exact care for collars, waistcoats, and beards. A lost wager soon sends him to Red Gap, a wild town in Washington state.

There Ruggles must learn American ways, from slang to saloons to self-reliance. Wilson mines the clash of English form and western freedom for laughs. Yet the comedy has heart, as Ruggles finds dignity in a new life. The novel remains a beloved classic of American humor.
capitola-the-madcap:
Mrs. Emma D. E. N. Southworth, a popular American storyteller, continued her hit The Hidden Hand in Capitola the Madcap, as Part Two. Capitola Black, called Cap, is an orphan girl raised in Virginia hills. Her guardian, Major Warfield, known as Old Hurricane, storms through scene after scene. Villainy circles the Hidden House and its captive.

Chapters send Cap into the Hidden Hollow to free a prisoner held in the house. Black Donald, the outlaw chief, matches wits with her across disguises and pursuits. A court-martial, a verdict, and the end of a border war widen the plot beyond Virginia. Clara Day's fate, Traverse Rocke's errand, and Colonel Le Noir's schemes weave through Cap's adventures. A mysterious maniac's story unlocks secrets near the close. Southworth ends with prospects brightening and Capitola turned capitalist, in her own coin. Dime-novel energy, cross-dressing escapes, and cliffhangers made Cap a heroine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gap:
Gap, a diocese in the Hautes-Alpes of France, was suppressed in 1801, joined to Digne, and restored in 1822 with much of old Embrun added. Its first bishop, by liturgical tradition, was Saint Demetrius, disciple of the apostles, though Duchesne counts Constantinus, seen at Epaone in 517, as the first bishop history can prove. The entry weighs legend against record throughout.

Gap's bishops include Aregius, who built a famed literary school prized by Gregory the Great, and Arnoux, set over a simoniac predecessor. Embrun's long roll runs from Marcellinus in the fourth century through Henry of Segusio, the canonist called Ostiensis. It reaches Jacques Gelu, an early believer in Joan of Arc, and Giulio de' Medici, later Clement VII. Tournon's college crowns the tale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-map:
Walter Map, sometimes wrongly written Maps, was Archdeacon of Oxford, born at or near Hereford about 1140 and dying between 1208 and 1210. Probably Welsh by extraction from the Marches, he became known through medieval church Latin and the Norman French of Henry II's court and law courts. At fourteen he went to Paris university, studying until 1160 under Girard la Pucelle, and by 1162 he was at England's court.

Henry made him a clerk of his household, implying he had taken or was about to take holy orders. Preferments followed: king's representative at the Third Lateran Council in 1179, where he disputed with the Waldensians, various benefices, and finally the Oxford archdeaconry in 1197. A failed bid for Hereford brought him into contact with St Hugh of Lincoln.
constance-dunlap:
Arthur B. Reeve's Constance Dunlap belongs to his Craig Kennedy series, though Kennedy stays offstage. Carlton Dunlap comes home late with the look of a hunted animal. His wife Constance, awake behind feigned sleep, hears his confession. He has forged, and the law is closing in.

Constance takes up crime to shield the husband she loves. The Forgers, The Embezzlers, The Gun Runners, and The Gamblers title her cases. She outwits detectives, fleeces plungers, and joins the criminals she studies. Reeve reverses his usual formula: the woman at the centre is the outlaw, not the scientist. Each episode is a complete caper with its own underworld trade explained. The book is a sympathetic portrait of a lady crook, written when that was a scandalous novelty. Constance's loyalty, not her loot, is the point Reeve keeps making.

doe-osti-3452085-myriad-world-baseline-g: How many people live where — and how old are they? The Myriad World Baseline provides global geodemographic estimates: population broken down by place and age group. Planners, researchers, and responders use these baselines to size everything from markets to missions.
madcap:
Madcap is a romantic adventure novel by George Gibbs. Its heroine is Hermia, and the first picture shows her teasing Mr. Markham. She tells him he must flirt and make pretty speeches. Chapters promise a gorilla, a marooning, and a rescue.

Olga Tcherny and the Fabiani family widen the plot's circle. There are mountebanks, a fairy godmother, and vagabond days. Danger comes, and with it a lady in the dark. Gibbs piles incident on incident in the old romantic manner. Hermia's madcap spirit drives every scene she enters. The book is light, swift, and full of improbable fun.
obed-hussey-who-of-all-inventors-made-br:
Follett L. Greeno edited Obed Hussey, Who, of All Inventors, Made Bread Cheap in 1912. Greeno calls it a true record of Hussey's life and struggles to introduce the reaper. Pamphlets by Hussey's friends and associates are reprinted here, with added facts and testimonials. Pictures show Hussey's American reaper and the inventor himself.

Hussey, of Quaker stock, was born in Maine in 1792 and moved early to Nantucket. Like other Nantucket boys he went whaling in his youth. Quiet and studious, he had a strong bent for intricate machines. He worked as a skillful draftsman at inventions all his life. A steam plow and a corn and cob mill stand among them.
ruggles-of-red-gap:
Harry Leon Wilson wrote Ruggles of Red Gap, dated 1915 and given to Helen Cooke Wilson. A front picture carries the line, I take it you failed to win the hundred pounds, sir. Chapter One opens at 6:30 in a Paris apartment, where the narrator, a valet, has just finished dressing the Honourable George. He is pleased, on the whole, with his work. Those last touches, he holds, mark the gap between a man well turned out and a man merely dressed.

Pride in craft runs through the opening talk, down to collars, waistcoats, and beards. The Honourable George's dress waistcoats no longer let him take a full breath, and his collars clasp too closely. The valet holds that a collar can give ample room if its depth is at least two and one quarter inches.
somewhere-in-red-gap:
Harry Leon Wilson sets Somewhere in Red Gap at the Arrowhead ranch, with pictures by John R. Neill, F. R. Gruger, and Henry Raleigh. The book, given to George Horace Lorimer, came out at New York from Grosset and Dunlap. Contents heads promise the Red Splash of Romance, Ma Pettengill and the Song of Songs, real Peruvian doughnuts, Cousin Egbert stepping in, and a piece called Little Old New York.

Chapter I opens in the big living room of the ranch house. Its walls are decked here and there with the prizes of the owner, Mrs. Lysander John Pettengill. Among them hang family portraits in crayon and cuts of noble beasts clipped from the Breeder's Gazette. One cut shows her standing on the centre table to see herself in the glass over the mantel.
the-submarine-boys-and-the-middies-the-p: Victor G. Durham's third book of the Submarine Boys series, dated 1909, sends Jack Benson and his friends to Annapolis as a prize detail. Only the title page and the heading of chapter one appear in this record. A contents list of twenty-four chapters stands with them. The cruise itself does not appear. The titles promise varied episodes. Eph flirts with science in one. Two kinds of voodoo appear. The boys squint at the Camelroorelephant. Marines hold men up. A companion Saalfield record lists only twenty chapters.
the-voyage-of-the-rattletrap: Hayden Carruth published The Voyage of the Rattletrap with Harper and Brothers in New York in 1897, illustrated by H. M. Wilder. He dedicates the book to John Briar, a poor cook but a good fellow. The pages present here hold the title page, contents, and illustrations list, so the journey's narrative does not appear. Chapter headings trace a wagon route from Lookout Lake to the Missouri River, into Nebraska, and across the Niobrara. Later chapters cross the sand hills toward the Black Hills and Deadwood, then turn homeward bound.
the-world-war-and-what-was-behind-it-or-: L. P. Bénézet, a school superintendent in Evansville, Indiana, wrote The World War and What Was Behind It. A contents list of twenty-six chapters is present here, without the chapters themselves. His subtitle calls the book the story of the map of Europe. Chapters run from Rome and the barbarian tribes to the war's cost. Bismarck appears as the Man of Blood and Iron. A closing chapter asks what Germany must learn.
theory-of-silk-weaving-a-treatise-on-the: Arnold Wolfensberger, a graduate of the Textile Institute of Zurich, wrote a treatise on silk weaving published in New York in 1921. The second revised and enlarged edition contains ninety-five plates. Its subject is the construction and application of weaves for broad and narrow silk fabrics. Plain, novelty, and Jacquard fabrics all fall within its scope, along with decomposition and calculation of weaves. A heading for drawing-in appears on page five. The opening pages and title matter are what is present here, so Wolfensberger's instructions themselves are not shown.
